title: The craft story
summary: Narrate the soldering milestone as a process story with the danger and the care both in it, then debate dangerous tools in the very week you got one.

steps.title: What a process story is
steps.body:
This week you tell a craft story: the story of a thing changing from sketch to ink. A process story is not a list of steps. Nobody wants to hear then I soldered the resistor, then I soldered the LED. They want to hear a thing change in your hands.

The shape, five beats: the wish, a circuit that lasts. The rules, danger named out loud and care chosen on purpose. The practice, ten joints on scrap and the cold one among them. The moment, the beat where it turned, maybe the first joint that froze into a shiny cone, maybe the LED lighting on solder for the first time. And the object, the badge itself, held up to the camera at the end.

Here is what makes a craft story honest: the danger stays in it, told straight. A story that hides the hot iron is a toy story, and a story that turns the iron into a monster is a scary story. A craft story does neither. It says: this tool can burn me, here is exactly what we did about that, and that is why I got to use it.

The philosophy question of the week rides along: why do finished things feel different from drafts? Your breadboard gate and your badge are the same circuit. One of them feels different in your hand. Keep the question simmering while you build the talk. Your story ends on your answer.

Voice rules, same three as always: speak to the back wall, pause after the sentence that matters most, look at one person per sentence.

steps.title: Build the story
steps.body:
On the whiteboard, write the five beats down the left edge: wish, rules, practice, moment, object. Next to each, one line only, in your own words, from your own bench today. No beat may be borrowed from how it was supposed to go: the practice beat must contain the joint that actually went wrong, and what care did about it.

Find your pause. Somewhere in the story is the sentence that matters most, probably in the moment beat. Mark it on the whiteboard. When you say it, stop for a full breath before going on and let it land.

Write your last line: your answer to why finished things feel different from drafts. Do not polish it into a greeting card. Say what you actually noticed when the badge lit.

Practise the whole story twice with a timer, badge in hand, aiming for two minutes. If it runs long, cut lines from the beat you love most, because that is where extra sentences hide.
checklist: Five beats on the whiteboard, each one line, each from what really happened
The practice beat includes the joint that went wrong and the fix
The danger is in the story, said calm, neither hidden nor turned into a monster
Two timed run-throughs done, with the pause landing after my marked sentence
The story ends on my own answer to why finished things feel different from drafts

steps.title: Before the debate: the steelman earns its keep
steps.body:
The motion is: dangerous tools should be for grown-ups only. And here is the delicious part: you are debating it in the very week a soldering iron came to your bench.

The steelman rule, same as always: before your first round, you state the other side's best case so well that the other side nods. This week the rule has teeth. If you argue against the motion, you must first make the honest case for it, and that case is sitting warm on your bench: an iron hot enough to melt metal was in a child's hands an hour ago, and burns do not care how clever the hands are. If you argue for the motion, you must first steelman the other side: that the safest tool user is one who learned the rules young, beside an adult, with a tool they respect.

Notice that your Build morning is evidence for both sides. That is what makes this a real debate and not a performance. Pick your side because you believe it, then earn it.

steps.title: Record it
steps.prompt: Record the craft story in one take: badge in hand, whole face visible, the pause landing where you marked it, ending on your drafts-versus-finished answer.
